p: Most people who come off the course early don't fall because their legs give way. It's their grip. Hanging and swinging use the hands and forearms far more than everyday life does, so a bit of preparation helps. If your kids are keen, a few goes on the monkey bars at the local park in the week before will make a noticeable difference, and the same goes for adults.

On the day, pace yourself. It's tempting to throw everything at the first run, but you'll get more out of the session by having a steady go at each obstacle, resting between attempts and saving a big effort for the end. Watching how others tackle a section is a great way to pick up tricks, too.

Bristol makes it easy to turn a session into a full day. Down on the harbourside, Bristol Aquarium is a calmer indoor option, and the little yellow and blue harbour ferries are a fun way to hop between stops along the water. Ashton Court Estate, on the edge of the city, has deer park walks and huge open spaces, and it's where the famous Bristol International Balloon Fiesta takes off every August.

Animal lovers can head out to the Bristol Zoo Project, near the M5, where the old city zoo has moved to a much bigger site with plenty of room for its residents. It's a full day on its own, so save it for another trip if you've already been hanging off rings all morning.
After a session, a proper meal is a must. Bristol's food scene is famously good, from street food stalls to family-friendly places along the waterfront, so you won't be short of choice.
